chapter_note.about: Analytical aptitude is reasoning from given facts, with no outside knowledge. You match relations in analogies, apply all, some and no with circles, and fill grids for seating and ranking. You find the rule in a series, test statements for truth, turn stories into graphs and trees, and use if-then rules safely. Every topic has a mechanical method, so the marks come from using it without skipping a clue.

concept_map.title: Analogies
concept_map.one_line: Say the exact relation of the first pair, then apply it to the second.

concept_map.title: Syllogisms
concept_map.one_line: Draw each premise as circles, and keep only conclusions true in every possible picture.

concept_map.title: Arrangements and rankings
concept_map.one_line: Build a people-by-seats table, apply each clue, and fix any person left with one seat.

concept_map.title: Series and coding
concept_map.one_line: Take differences, then second differences, then ratios, then split into alternating terms.

concept_map.title: Truth and statement puzzles
concept_map.one_line: Assume one statement is true, test the rest, and flip on a clash.

concept_map.title: Graph and route reasoning
concept_map.one_line: Turn the story into nodes and edges, then test the property on the sketch.

concept_map.title: Family relations
concept_map.one_line: Draw parents above children, add each clue as an edge, and read the path asked.

concept_map.title: Conditional logic
concept_map.one_line: Write the rule as P implies Q, then use the contrapositive and reject the converse.

chapter_note.simple: Analytical aptitude is solving puzzles with clues. You might fill a grid of who sits where, find the rule in a list of numbers, or work out who is lying by trying each guess. The main habit is to write things down, such as a table, circles, a family tree or a small graph, instead of holding it in your head. Another habit is to test every clue before you answer, because the first answer that fits is often not the only one. For if-then rules, remember that you can run the rule backwards only by flipping and negating it.

cards.title: Analogies
cards.simple: An analogy says 'these two things are related in the same way as those two'. A tail belongs to a dog. A wing belongs to a bird. The link is 'part of a whole', so the answer is bird. The skill is to put the link into a few words before you look at the options, because the options are designed to tempt you with words on the same topic. In exam words: find the relation (part to whole, function, degree, item to group), then pick the option that has the same relation in the same order.
cards.idea: Tail : Dog :: Wing : ?  A tail is a part of a dog. A wing is a part of a bird. The link is **part to whole**, so the answer is bird. Say the link in a short phrase first. Then test each option against that phrase, and check that the order of the pair is the same.
cards.idea_full:
Tail : Dog :: Wing : ?  A tail is a part of a dog. A wing is a part of a bird. The link is **part to whole**, so the answer is bird. Say the link in a short phrase first. Then test each option against that phrase, and check that the order of the pair is the same.

The common links are synonym, opposite, degree, part to whole, function (what something does or makes), and item to group. A word on the same topic but with a different link is a decoy.
cards.definition:
A : B :: C : ? means 'A is to B as C is to ?'.

Common relations: part : whole (tail : dog), function : product (lamp : light), item : group (book : library), tool : action (pen : write), synonym, antonym and degree (warm : hot).

The same relation must hold in the same direction for both pairs.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the first pair as a rule that you must be able to state in words, like 'the second word is the whole that the first word belongs to'. The second pair has to obey the same rule. If you cannot say the rule in one short phrase, you do not understand the pair yet. Decoys rely on this: they share a subject with the stem (dog and bone, bird and feather) but follow a different rule. Direction matters too. 'Tail : Dog' is part then whole, so 'Wing : Bird' fits, but 'Bird : Wing' would be whole then part.

example.setup: Tail : Dog :: Wing : ? (Bird / Feather / Sky / Fly)
steps: Name the link of the first pair: a tail is a part of a dog. Part to whole.
Apply to the second pair: a wing is a part of what whole?
Bird is the whole. Feather is a part of a wing, which is the wrong direction. Sky and fly are only related by topic.
Choose bird.

examples.setup: Tail : Dog :: Wing : ? (Bird / Feather / Sky / Fly)
steps: Name the link of the first pair: a tail is a part of a dog. Part to whole.
Apply to the second pair: a wing is a part of what whole?
Bird is the whole. Feather is a part of a wing, which is the wrong direction. Sky and fly are only related by topic.
Choose bird.

examples.setup: Lamp : Light :: Fan : ? (Air / Switch / Blade / Summer)
steps: Name the link: a lamp produces light. Function to product.
Apply to the fan: what does a fan produce?
A fan produces moving air. A switch and a blade are parts, and summer is a topic word.
Choose air.

examples.setup: Book : Library :: Tree : ? (Wood / Forest / Leaf / Garden)
steps: Name the link: a library is a collection made of many books. Item to group.
Apply to tree: a collection made of many trees.
A forest is a collection of trees. Wood is a material, and a leaf is a part. A garden holds plants of many kinds.
Choose forest.
examples.answer: Forest. Wood and leaf come from a tree, but they do not describe a group of trees.

cards.why: Analogies appear as a quick 1-mark question. A named relation removes the decoys. In GATE: a pair of words and a blank, with options that share the topic of the second pair.
how: Say the link of the first pair in a short phrase.
Check the order of the pair (A to B).
Apply the phrase to the second pair.
Strike options that only share a topic, and pick the one with the same link.
cards.mistake: Choosing the word that belongs to the same topic. A feather goes with a bird but is not what a wing is a part of. Match the relation and its direction, not the topic.
edge_cases: A pair can have two links, so pick the one that also fits the second pair.
Reversed pairs (whole : part) need the reversed link.
Degree analogies need the same step size and direction.
A function link can be to a product (lamp : light) or to an action (pen : write).

cards.title: Syllogisms
cards.simple: A syllogism is a little logic puzzle with 'all', 'some' and 'no'. Draw circles. If all roses are flowers, the rose circle sits inside the flower circle. If all flowers are plants, the flower circle sits inside the plant circle. So the rose circle must be inside the plant circle: all roses are plants. A conclusion counts only if it is true in every way you could draw the circles. In exam words: represent premises with Venn circles, and accept a conclusion only if it holds in all diagrams consistent with the premises.
cards.idea: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Draw rose inside flower inside plant. So all roses are plants must be true, and 'all plants are roses' need not be. **Draw the circles**, and accept a conclusion only if it is true in every picture the premises allow.
cards.idea_full:
All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Draw rose inside flower inside plant. So all roses are plants must be true, and 'all plants are roses' need not be.

**Draw the circles**, and accept a conclusion only if it is true in every picture the premises allow. 'Some' in a premise does not turn into 'all' in the conclusion. Try the loosest picture, where circles overlap as little as the premises allow.
cards.definition:
All A are B: circle A inside circle B.

No A is B: circles A and B apart.

Some A are B: circles overlap (at least one member in both).

Some A are not B: part of A lies outside B.

A conclusion follows only if it holds in every diagram consistent with the premises. Note: 'Some A are B' also allows 'All A are B' as one possible picture, unless the premises say otherwise.
cards.intuition_full: A premise is a restriction on how the circles may sit, not a full picture. 'Some books are pens' only forces a small overlap. The circles could overlap a little, a lot, or one could sit entirely inside the other. A conclusion must survive every such arrangement. The trick is to look for the arrangement that breaks the conclusion. If you can draw one picture where the premises hold and the conclusion fails, the conclusion does not follow. 'All' chains are the exception, since they force a nesting of circles. With 'no', the circles must stay apart, so conclusions of the form 'some X are not Y' can follow for the circle that touches the premise.

example.setup: Premises: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Conclusions: I. All roses are plants. II. All plants are roses.
steps: Draw the roses circle inside the flowers circle.
Draw the flowers circle inside the plants circle.
So roses lie inside plants: Conclusion I holds in every picture.
Plants can contain things that are not roses, such as grass. So II fails in a legitimate picture.

examples.setup: Premises: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Conclusions: I. All roses are plants. II. All plants are roses.
steps: Draw the roses circle inside the flowers circle.
Draw the flowers circle inside the plants circle.
So roses lie inside plants: Conclusion I holds in every picture.
Plants can contain things that are not roses, such as grass. So II fails in a legitimate picture.

examples.setup: Premises: Some books are pens. All pens are tools. Conclusions: I. Some books are tools. II. All books are tools.
steps: Some books overlap with pens, so draw an overlap.
All pens are inside tools, so the overlap sits inside tools too.
Those books that are pens are tools, so some books are tools: I follows.
Other books may lie outside tools, so II does not follow.

examples.setup: Premises: No fish is a bird. Some birds are swimmers. Conclusions: I. Some swimmers are not fish. II. No swimmer is a fish.
steps: Draw fish and bird circles apart.
Some birds are swimmers, so the swimmers circle overlaps the birds circle.
The swimmers that are birds are outside the fish circle, so some swimmers are not fish: I follows.
Nothing stops the swimmers circle from also overlapping fish, because a swimmer can be a fish too. So II does not follow.

cards.why: Syllogisms test whether you reason from what is given and not from what seems true. The circles stop you from over-reading 'some'. In GATE: two premises and two or three conclusions, with options like 'only I follows' or 'both follow'.
how: Draw one circle diagram per premise.
Combine them, and sketch the loosest picture too.
Test each conclusion in every picture.
Pick the conclusions that always hold.
cards.mistake: Treating 'some' as 'all'. From 'Some graduates are artists' you cannot conclude that all graduates are artists. A conclusion must hold in the loosest picture, not only in the neat one.
edge_cases: 'Some A are B' and 'some B are A' are equivalent.
'All A are B' does not give 'all B are A'.
'Some A are not B' can be true even when 'some A are B' is true.
Two 'some' premises usually give no conclusion.
connections: Reading inference (ga.verbal v7) uses the same all, some, none logic.
Conditionals (n8) are the same as 'all' statements.
Venn diagrams in sets (dm.sets_rel) formalise circles.

check.q: All A are B. Does 'some B are A' follow?
check.a: Yes. If A is inside B and A is non-empty, they share members.

check.q: Some A are B. Does 'all A are B' follow?
No cat is a dog. Does 'no dog is a cat' follow?

cards.title: Arrangements and rankings
cards.simple: Imagine four friends and four seats in a row, and a few clues about who can sit where. Draw a little grid with the people down the side and the seats along the top. Each clue lets you cross out some boxes. When a person has only one box left, they must sit there, so you cross that seat out for everyone else. Keep going until every clue is used. In exam words: make a people-by-position table, eliminate with each clue, fix singletons, and check the final arrangement against all clues.
cards.idea: Four people A, B, C, D sit in four seats in a row. Clues: A is at an end, B is immediately right of A, D is not next to B. Draw a people-by-seats grid and cross out boxes with each clue. When a person has one box left, **fix** them and cross that seat out for everyone else. Keep going until every clue is used.
cards.idea_full:
Four people A, B, C, D sit in four seats in a row. Clues: A is at an end, B is immediately right of A, D is not next to B. Draw a people-by-seats grid and cross out boxes with each clue. When a person has one box left, **fix** them and cross that seat out for everyone else.

Keep going until every clue is used, not until one arrangement works. For circles, count positions modulo the number of seats, and remember that left and right depend on which way the person faces.
cards.definition:
Table: rows are people, columns are seats. x means impossible, a tick means fixed.

A singleton is a person with exactly one open seat, or a seat with exactly one open person. Fix it and eliminate in its row and column.

Ranking: if a person is p-th from the left in a row of n, they are (n - p + 1)-th from the right. People between two positions p < q number q - p - 1.

Circle with n seats: the person opposite is n/2 seats away. Left and right are from the seated person's point of view.
cards.intuition_full: Every clue removes possibilities. The grid is a way to remember exactly which possibilities remain, so nothing is tracked in your head. The key move is the singleton rule: once one person is forced into a seat, that seat is gone for everyone else, which may force another person, and so on like dominoes. This is why you should not stop at the first arrangement that fits some clues. Another arrangement may also satisfy them until the last clue rules it out. For rankings, the from-left and from-right positions always add to n + 1, which converts between the two. In circles, left and right depend on the direction the person faces, and 'opposite' always means n/2 seats away.

example.setup: Four people A, B, C, D sit in seats 1 to 4 in a row. Clues: (1) A sits at an end. (2) B sits immediately to the right of A. (3) D is not next to B. Find the order.
steps: Four people, four seats. Each cell asks: can this person sit here? Start with every cell open.
Clue 1: A sits at an end. A cannot take seat 2 or 3.
Clue 2: B is immediately right of A. Seat 4 has nothing to its right, so A is in seat 1 and B in seat 2. Seats 1 and 2 are now taken, so C and D lose them.
Clue 3: D is not next to B. B is in seat 2, so seat 3 is next to it. D cannot sit there, so D takes seat 4 and C gets seat 3.
Every row and column has exactly one yes. The order is A, B, C, D. Check each clue against it before answering.

examples.setup: Four people A, B, C, D sit in seats 1 to 4 in a row. Clues: (1) A sits at an end. (2) B sits immediately to the right of A. (3) D is not next to B. Find the order.
steps: Four people, four seats. Each cell asks: can this person sit here? Start with every cell open.
Clue 1: A sits at an end. A cannot take seat 2 or 3.
Clue 2: B is immediately right of A. Seat 4 has nothing to its right, so A is in seat 1 and B in seat 2. Seats 1 and 2 are now taken, so C and D lose them.
Clue 3: D is not next to B. B is in seat 2, so seat 3 is next to it. D cannot sit there, so D takes seat 4 and C gets seat 3.
Every row and column has exactly one yes. The order is A, B, C, D. Check each clue against it before answering.

examples.setup: In a row of 30 students, A is 12th from the left and B is 9th from the right. How many students stand between A and B?
steps: Convert B to a position from the left: 30 - 9 + 1 = 22.
So A is at position 12 and B at position 22.
Students between: 22 - 12 - 1 = 9.
examples.answer: 9. Check by counting positions 13 to 21, which is 9 students.

examples.setup: Eight people sit around a table facing the centre. Q sits third to the left of P, and R sits immediately to the left of Q. Who sits opposite P?
steps: Count seats to the left of P: Q is 3 seats away, so R is 4 seats away.
With 8 seats, the person opposite is 8/2 = 4 seats away.
So R is opposite P.
Counting to the right instead would put the opposite seat 4 away too, but Q and R would sit on the other side of the table.
examples.answer: R. Always count left and right from the seated person's view, not your own.

cards.why: Arrangement puzzles are the most common analytical question. A grid turns a tangled story into mechanical elimination. In GATE: seating, ranking and ordering puzzles, with case analysis.
how: List the people and positions, and draw the grid.
Apply each clue and mark x for impossible cells.
Fix singletons, then repeat the elimination.
Check the final arrangement against every clue.
cards.mistake: Stopping at the first arrangement that fits, or using your own left and right instead of the seated person's. Another arrangement may satisfy most clues. Use all clues and re-check the final answer.
edge_cases: In a ranking, 'p-th from left' and 'q-th from right' sum to n + 1 only if they refer to the same person.
Circular arrangements have no fixed first seat, so fix one person.
'Immediately to the left' leaves no seat between.
A clue like 'not next to' removes two neighbouring seats.
connections: Truth puzzles (n5) use the same case-by-case elimination.
Counting (ga.quant a8) gives the number of arrangements.
Constraint satisfaction in AI (ai.logic) is this same elimination.

check.q: In a row of 25, P is 7th from the left. What is P's position from the right?
6 people sit around a table. Who is opposite the person at seat 2?
A is taller than B, B is taller than C. Who is shortest?

**Worked example.** Four people A, B, C, D sit in seats 1 to 4 in a row. Clues: (1) A sits at an end. (2) B sits immediately to the right of A. (3) D is not next to B. Find the order.

**Answer:** A, B, C, D (seats 1 to 4).

**Check yourself:** In a row of 25, P is 7th from the left. What is P's position from the right?

*Answer:* 25 - 7 + 1 = 19th.

cards.title: Series and coding
cards.simple: A number series hides a rule. To find it, look at the gaps between neighbours. For 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 the gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9, which keep growing by 2. When the gaps themselves grow by a steady amount, the next gap is 11, so the next number is 26 + 11 = 37. If the gaps do not show a pattern, try multiplying, or look at every second number separately. In exam words: first differences, then second differences, then ratios, then interleaved odd and even terms.
cards.idea: What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? Look at the gaps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not equal, but the gaps of the gaps are all 2. So the next gap is 9 + 2 = 11, and the next term is 26 + 11 = 37. Use a **ladder of differences**: differences, then differences again, then ratios, then alternating terms.
cards.idea_full:
What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? Look at the gaps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not equal, but the gaps of the gaps are all 2. So the next gap is 9 + 2 = 11, and the next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared plus 1.

Use a **ladder of differences**: differences, then differences again, then ratios, then alternating terms. For letter codes, shift each letter by a fixed number, or map letters to positions (A = 1, B = 2).
cards.definition:
First difference constant: arithmetic series, a_n = a + (n - 1)d.

Second difference constant: quadratic, so the first differences form an arithmetic series.

Constant ratio: geometric series, a_n = a r^(n-1).

If nothing fits, split into two series made of the odd-position and even-position terms.

Letter codes: replace each letter by its position (A = 1 to Z = 26) and look for a pattern in the numbers.
cards.intuition_full: A differences table is like checking the speed and then the acceleration of a moving object. If the first gaps are steady, the series moves at constant speed (arithmetic). If the gaps change by a steady amount, the speed has constant acceleration, which gives a quadratic pattern such as n² + 1. If ratios between neighbours are steady, the series multiplies (geometric). Some puzzles weave two rules together, such as 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16 where the odd positions double and the even positions double from 3. Always test the simple ideas first, in order, and only then move to the odd ones. A single rule across all terms is not guaranteed.

steps: What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? First try the gaps between neighbours.
Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not constant, so it is not a plain add-the-same rule.
Differences of the differences: 2, 2, 2. A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern.
Extend from the bottom. The second difference stays 2.
So the next first difference is 9 + 2 = 11.
The next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37.

examples.setup: Find the next term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26.
steps: What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? First try the gaps between neighbours.
Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not constant, so it is not a plain add-the-same rule.
Differences of the differences: 2, 2, 2. A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern.
Extend from the bottom. The second difference stays 2.
So the next first difference is 9 + 2 = 11.
The next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37.

examples.setup: Find the next term of 3, 4, 8, 17, 33.
steps: First differences: 1, 4, 9, 16.
These are perfect squares: 1², 2², 3², 4².
The next difference is 5² = 25.
Next term: 33 + 25 = 58.
examples.answer: 58. The gaps themselves follow a rule.

examples.setup: Find the next term of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16.
steps: The differences are 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, and the second differences are not constant, so a simple rule does not fit.
Split into two series. Odd positions: 2, 4, 8, 16 (doubling). Even positions: 3, 6, 12 (doubling).
The next term is in an even position, so continue 3, 6, 12 by doubling: 24.

cards.why: Series and coding questions are short pattern hunts. The difference ladder finds the rule quickly. In GATE: a number series, a letter code, or a table with a rule per row or column.
how: Write the differences between neighbours.
If not constant, difference again, then test ratios.
If still no rule, split into odd and even positions.
Verify the rule on every given term before using it.
cards.mistake: Assuming one rule across all the terms, or stopping when a rule fits only some terms. If the differences look random, test the odd and even positions separately and then check the rule fits every term.
edge_cases: Differences can themselves be a geometric series.
Letter-code questions may wrap around from Z to A.
A series can mix operations, such as multiply by 2 then add 1.
Table rules may differ per row, so check each row.
connections: Series in aptitude (ga.quant a12) uses the GP and AP sums.
Recurrences (dm.recurrence) describe the same rules formally.
Limits (calc.limits) study how series behave as terms go on.

check.q: Find the next term of 5, 9, 13, 17.
Find the next term of 2, 6, 18, 54.
Code each letter +1: what is 'MAT'?

try.label: Try the first series and coding question (L1)

cards.what: What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? Look at the gaps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not equal, but the gaps of the gaps are all 2. So the next gap is 9 + 2 = 11, and the next term is 26 + 11 = 37. Use a **ladder of differences**: differences, then differences again, then ratios, then alternating terms.
cards.what_full:
What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? Look at the gaps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not equal, but the gaps of the gaps are all 2. So the next gap is 9 + 2 = 11, and the next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared plus 1.

Use a **ladder of differences**: differences, then differences again, then ratios, then alternating terms. For letter codes, shift each letter by a fixed number, or map letters to positions (A = 1, B = 2).

First difference constant: arithmetic series, a_n = a + (n - 1)d.

Second difference constant: quadratic, so the first differences form an arithmetic series.

Constant ratio: geometric series, a_n = a r^(n-1).

If nothing fits, split into two series made of the odd-position and even-position terms.

Letter codes: replace each letter by its position (A = 1 to Z = 26) and look for a pattern in the numbers.

**Worked example.** Find the next term of 2, 5, 10, 17, 26.

1. What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? First try the gaps between neighbours.
2. Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not constant, so it is not a plain add-the-same rule.
3. Differences of the differences: 2, 2, 2. A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern.
4. Extend from the bottom. The second difference stays 2.
5. So the next first difference is 9 + 2 = 11.
6. The next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37.

**Answer:** 37.

**Check yourself:** Find the next term of 5, 9, 13, 17.

*Answer:* 21 (constant difference 4).
cards.trap: Assuming one rule across all the terms, or stopping when a rule fits only some terms. If the differences look random, test the odd and even positions separately and then check the rule fits every term.
cards.why_full:
Series and coding questions are short pattern hunts. The difference ladder finds the rule quickly. In GATE: a number series, a letter code, or a table with a rule per row or column.

cards.title: Truth and statement puzzles
cards.simple: In these puzzles some people always tell the truth (knights) and some always lie (knaves). You cannot know who is who, so you guess and test. Say you guess A is a knight. Then whatever A says must be true, and that tells you something about B. If you hit a clash, your guess was wrong, so flip it. Write each guess as a short row and check every statement. In exam words: try each assumption for one person, propagate the consequences, and keep the assignment where every statement is consistent.
cards.idea: A says 'B is a knave'. B says 'we are both knights'. Knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie. Guess A is a knight. Then B is a knave, and B's statement is false, which is consistent. Try the other guess, and it clashes. Write each guess as a row and **check every statement**.
cards.idea_full:
A says 'B is a knave'. B says 'we are both knights'. Knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie. Guess A is a knight. Then B is a knave, and B's statement is false, which is consistent. Try the other guess (A is a knave), and it clashes. Write each guess as a row and **check every statement**.

For 'exactly one statement is true' puzzles, assume each suspect is guilty in turn, count the true statements, and keep the case that gives exactly one.
cards.definition:
Knight: every statement is true. Knave: every statement is false.

A statement is true exactly when the person making it is a knight.

Method: pick a variable (who is a knight, or who is guilty), assume a value, evaluate every statement, and accept the assumption only if all statements are consistent with it.

If both assumptions for one person survive, use another person's statement to separate them.
cards.intuition_full: The rule 'knights say true things and knaves say false things' links each person's type to the truth of their statement. So a guess about one person ripples out to others through the statements. If the ripple ever contradicts the guess, the guess is wrong. With only two types per person, a puzzle with three people has at most eight assignments, so careful case checking always finishes. For 'exactly one statement is true' puzzles, the unknown is usually who did it. Test each suspect in turn, evaluate all statements for that suspect, and count. Do not stop at the first case that fits some statements. A second case may also fit, and only one should satisfy the count.

example.setup: A says: 'B is a knave.' B says: 'We are both knights.' Who is who?
steps: Assume A is a knight. Then A's statement is true, so B is a knave.
B is a knave, so B's statement is false: it is not true that both are knights. This is consistent, since A is a knight and B is a knave.
Try the other case: A is a knave. Then B is not a knave, so B is a knight, and B's statement says both are knights, but A is a knave. Contradiction.
Only the first assignment survives.
example.answer: A is a knight and B is a knave.

examples.setup: A says: 'B is a knave.' B says: 'We are both knights.' Who is who?
steps: Assume A is a knight. Then A's statement is true, so B is a knave.
B is a knave, so B's statement is false: it is not true that both are knights. This is consistent, since A is a knight and B is a knave.
Try the other case: A is a knave. Then B is not a knave, so B is a knight, and B's statement says both are knights, but A is a knave. Contradiction.
Only the first assignment survives.
examples.answer: A is a knight and B is a knave.

examples.setup: Exactly one of X, Y, Z took the pen, and exactly one of these statements is true. X: 'Y took it.' Y: 'I did not take it.' Z: 'X is lying.' Who took it?
steps: Test X as the thief. X's statement is false, Y's is true, Z's (X lies) is true. Two true statements, so X is not the thief.
Test Y as the thief. X's statement is true, Y's is false, Z's is false (X is not lying). One true statement: consistent.
Test Z as the thief. X's is false, Y's is true, Z's is true. Two true, so no.
Only Y gives exactly one true statement.

examples.setup: A says: 'B is a liar.' B says: 'C is a liar.' C says: 'A and B are both liars.' Each person is a truth-teller or a liar. Who is who?
steps: Start with A as truthful. Then B is a liar, so B's statement is false and C is not a liar. C is truthful, so A and B are both liars, but A is truthful. Contradiction.
So A is a liar. A's statement is false, so B is truthful.
B is truthful, so C is a liar. Check C: 'A and B are both liars' is false, since B is truthful. This fits a liar.
Check A: 'B is a liar' is false, which fits a liar. All consistent.
examples.answer: A is a liar, B is truthful, C is a liar.

cards.why: Statement puzzles train careful case work. The methods are the same each time, and the traps come from stopping early. In GATE: who tells the truth, who did it, and 'exactly one statement is true' puzzles.
how: Choose one variable, such as one person's type or guilt.
Assume a value, and evaluate every statement.
If any statement contradicts the assumption, flip it.
Check the surviving case against all statements.
cards.mistake: Guessing, or stopping at the first case that fits some statements. Test both assumptions, and count true statements when the puzzle says 'exactly one'.
edge_cases: A knave's statement is false, so the opposite of it is true.
If both cases fit, the puzzle needs another clue.
'At least one of us is a knave' is true for a knight only if the other is a knave.
A person who says 'I am a liar' makes the puzzle impossible.
connections: Conditional logic (n8) gives the 'if then' behind each statement.
Arrangements (n3) use the same elimination style.
Boolean logic (dm.logic) formalises truth values.

check.q: A knight says 'I am a knight.' Is the statement true?
check.a: Yes, a knight tells the truth.

check.q: A knave says 'I am a knight.' Is that possible?
check.a: Yes. The statement is false, as a knave's must be.

check.q: A says 'B is a knight'. B says 'A and I are of different types'. Who is who?
check.a: If A is a knight, B is a knight, but then B's statement is false, a contradiction. So A is a knave, B is a knave, and B's statement is indeed false. Both are knaves.

2. B is a knave, so B's statement is false: it is not true that both are knights. This is consistent, since A is a knight and B is a knave.
3. Try the other case: A is a knave. Then B is not a knave, so B is a knight, and B's statement says both are knights, but A is a knave. Contradiction.
4. Only the first assignment survives.

**Check yourself:** A knight says 'I am a knight.' Is the statement true?

*Answer:* Yes, a knight tells the truth.

cards.title: Graph and route reasoning
cards.simple: When a puzzle talks about towns and roads, or people and friendships, draw dots and lines. Each town is a dot and each road is a line, and write the length or cost on the line. Then the question becomes a property of the picture: what is the shortest route, can you walk every road once, or how many colours do you need so that neighbours differ? For the shortest route, try the few routes by hand. In exam words: model as a graph with nodes and edges, then check paths, cycles, degrees or colourings.
cards.idea: Four towns A, B, C, D with roads A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Draw towns as dots and roads as weighted lines. The shortest route from A to D is a path with the smallest total. A-C-B-D costs 2 + 1 + 5 = 8, which beats the direct-looking options. Turn the story into a **graph**, then test the property.
cards.idea_full:
Four towns A, B, C, D with roads A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Draw towns as dots and roads as weighted lines. The shortest route from A to D is a path with the smallest total. A-C-B-D costs 2 + 1 + 5 = 8, which beats A-B-D (9) and A-C-D (10).

Turn the story into a **graph**: entities become nodes, links become edges. Then ask the question as a property: shortest path, a walk using every road once (Euler), a tour visiting every town once (Hamilton), or a colouring.
cards.definition:
Graph: nodes (vertices) joined by edges. Degree of a node: the number of edges at it.

Euler walk: uses every edge exactly once. It exists if the graph is connected and has 0 or 2 odd-degree nodes (2 means start and end at those).

Hamiltonian cycle: visits every node exactly once and returns.

Colouring: adjacent nodes get different colours. A ring (cycle) of even length needs 2 colours, of odd length needs 3.
cards.intuition_full: A graph strips a story to its structure. The names and the map shape do not matter, only who connects to whom. Many questions then become tiny search problems. For shortest paths, list the few candidate routes and add the weights, or grow the cheapest frontier like Dijkstra. For Euler walks, every time you pass through a node you use one edge to enter and one to leave, so interior nodes need even degree. Only the start and end nodes can have odd degree, hence the 0 or 2 odd nodes rule. For colouring, a ring of an odd number of nodes has no way to alternate two colours, so it needs 3.

example.setup: Roads: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Find the cheapest route cost from A to D.
steps: Draw A, B, C, D as dots and each road as a weighted line.
List the routes from A to D: A-B-D, A-C-D, A-C-B-D.
The smallest is 8.

examples.setup: Roads: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Find the cheapest route cost from A to D.
steps: Draw A, B, C, D as dots and each road as a weighted line.
List the routes from A to D: A-B-D, A-C-D, A-C-B-D.
The smallest is 8.

examples.setup: Roads: A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A and A-C. Can a traveller use every road exactly once?
steps: Draw the graph and count the degree of each town.
A has roads to B, D and C: degree 3. B has A and C: 2. C has B, D and A: 3. D has C and A: 2.
The odd-degree towns are A and C, exactly two.
So an Euler walk exists, starting at A and ending at C (or the reverse).
examples.answer: Yes, starting at A and ending at C.

examples.setup: Regions are arranged in a ring, each touching its two neighbours. How many colours are needed if the ring has 5 regions, and if it has 6?
steps: Model each region as a node, and each touching pair as an edge. The graph is a cycle.
For 6 regions: alternate two colours around the ring. 6 is even, so it closes up. 2 colours.
For 5 regions: alternate two colours and the last region touches both colours, so it needs a third. 3 colours.

cards.why: Graph questions in GATE aptitude are small. The skill is the translation from a story into nodes and edges. In GATE: shortest routes, tours and walks, colouring and bridges, usually with a figure.
how: Draw each entity as a node.
Draw each link as an edge, with weights if given.
Name the property (path, cycle, degree, colouring).
Test it on the sketch, and re-read the story for missed edges.
cards.mistake: Missing an edge or misreading a weight when drawing from the story. One missing road changes the answer. Re-read the story once after drawing, ticking each road.
edge_cases: An Euler walk needs a connected graph.
With 0 odd-degree nodes the walk can start anywhere and return.
The shortest path can use more edges than the direct road.
A cycle of odd length needs 3 colours.
connections: Graph algorithms (algo.shortest, ds.graphs) solve these at scale.
Discrete maths graphs (dm.graphs) give Euler and Hamilton results.
Truth puzzles (n5) and arrangements (n3) can be recast as graphs.

check.q: A graph has 4 nodes each of degree 3. Does an Euler walk exist?
check.a: No. It has four odd-degree nodes, more than 2.

check.q: What is the least number of colours for a ring of 4 regions?
Roads A-B 2, B-C 3, A-C 6. Cheapest route A to C?

Graph: nodes (vertices) joined by edges. Degree of a node: the number of edges at it.

Euler walk: uses every edge exactly once. It exists if the graph is connected and has 0 or 2 odd-degree nodes (2 means start and end at those).

Colouring: adjacent nodes get different colours. A ring (cycle) of even length needs 2 colours, of odd length needs 3.

**Worked example.** Roads: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8. Find the cheapest route cost from A to D.

1. Draw A, B, C, D as dots and each road as a weighted line.
2. List the routes from A to D: A-B-D, A-C-D, A-C-B-D.

4. The smallest is 8.

cards.title: Family relations
cards.simple: Family puzzles are easier if you draw a family tree. Put parents above their children and draw a line between married couples. Then add each clue one at a time. 'My mother's brother' means go up to the mother, then across to her brother. Do not guess whether a person is a man or a woman unless the question tells you. Then read the question as a path along the tree. In exam words: draw a tree with parent edges downward and spouse links sideways, translate each phrase to an edge, and read off the relation.
cards.idea: A is B's mother's brother. Draw B, then B's mother above, then the mother's brother beside her. A is B's **maternal uncle**. Draw parents above children, add each clue as a line, and read the question as a path on the tree. Never assume a person's gender unless the question says so.
cards.idea_full:
A is B's mother's brother. Draw B, then B's mother above, then the mother's brother beside her. A is B's **maternal uncle**. Draw parents above children, add each clue as a line, and read the question as a path on the tree.

Never assume a person's gender unless the question says so. 'Sibling' and 'child' do not tell the gender. Write the relation as the shortest path: up, across, down.
cards.definition:
Tree conventions: parent above child, siblings on one level, spouses linked sideways.

Path words: up = parent, across = sibling or spouse, down = child.

Useful names: father's or mother's brother = uncle, father's or mother's sister = aunt, uncle's or aunt's child = cousin, spouse's sibling = brother-in-law or sister-in-law.

If gender is unknown, use neutral words (sibling, child, parent).
cards.intuition_full: A family tree turns words into geometry. 'Mother of' means go up. 'Brother of' means move sideways to the same generation. 'Son of' means go down. Every clue is one step, and the question asks for the total journey. The usual errors come from invented details: assuming a sibling is a brother, or that a 'cousin' is on the mother's side. Write only what is given. When gender is not stated, answers such as aunt or uncle cannot be told apart, so the correct option is the neutral one if the question is built that way.

example.setup: A is B's mother's brother. How is A related to B?
steps: Draw B at the bottom.
Go up one step to B's mother.
Go sideways to her brother, who is A.
The path is up, across: A is B's maternal uncle.

examples.setup: A is B's mother's brother. How is A related to B?
steps: Draw B at the bottom.
Go up one step to B's mother.
Go sideways to her brother, who is A.
The path is up, across: A is B's maternal uncle.

examples.setup: P is the father of Q. R is the sister of P. S is the son of R. How is S related to Q?
steps: Draw P with child Q.
R is P's sister, so R is on P's level.
S is R's son, one level below R.
Q and S are both children of siblings (P and R), so they are cousins.

examples.setup: A is the child of B's sibling. How is B related to A?
steps: Draw B's sibling above A, and B beside that sibling.
B is a parent's sibling of A.
The question gives no gender for B, so B can be an uncle or an aunt.
The neutral answer is parent's sibling.
examples.answer: B is A's uncle or aunt (gender not stated).

cards.why: Family-relation questions are one or two marks in recent GATE papers. A tree removes the confusion in long chains. In GATE: a chain of relations and a question asking how two people are related.
how: Draw the generations, parents above children.
Add each clue as a link, and keep gender open unless stated.
Find the two people the question asks about.
Read the relation from the path between them.
cards.mistake: Assuming genders the question did not give. A 'sibling' may be a brother or sister. Keep the neutral term unless the clue states otherwise.
edge_cases: 'Maternal' and 'paternal' say which parent's side.
Cousins share grandparents but not parents.
A spouse's sibling is an in-law.
Step relatives need an explicit remarriage.
connections: Analogies (n1) also rely on naming relations precisely.
Graph reasoning (n6): a tree is a graph with a direction.
Sets and relations (dm.sets_rel) formalise 'is a parent of'.

check.q: A is the father of B, and B is the sister of C. How is A related to C?
A's mother is the sister of B. How is B related to A?
check.a: Maternal aunt or uncle (B's gender is not given).

check.q: X's son is Y's brother. How is X related to Y?
check.a: Y's father or mother (X's gender is not given).

cards.what: A is B's mother's brother. Draw B, then B's mother above, then the mother's brother beside her. A is B's **maternal uncle**. Draw parents above children, add each clue as a line, and read the question as a path on the tree. Never assume a person's gender unless the question says so.

**Answer:** Maternal uncle.

**Check yourself:** A is the father of B, and B is the sister of C. How is A related to C?

*Answer:* Father.

cards.title: Conditional logic
cards.simple: 'If it rains, the ground is wet.' If you see a dry ground, you know it did not rain, because rain would have made it wet. That backwards step is called the contrapositive, and it is always safe. But seeing a wet ground does not prove it rained, since a hose could have done it. That backwards-the-wrong-way step is the converse, and it is not safe. Rules can also be chained: rain gives wet ground, wet ground gives slippery, so rain gives slippery. In exam words: P implies Q is equivalent to not Q implies not P, but not equivalent to Q implies P.
cards.idea: Two rules: if P then Q, and if Q then R. Suppose we learn R is false. Then Q must be false, because Q true would force R true. And then P must be false for the same reason. The safe backward step is the **contrapositive**: not Q implies not P. The converse, Q implies P, is a different claim and is not guaranteed.
cards.idea_full:
Two rules: if P then Q, and if Q then R. Suppose we learn R is false. Then Q must be false, because Q true would force R true. And then P must be false for the same reason. The safe backward step is the **contrapositive**: not Q implies not P. The converse, Q implies P, is a different claim and is not guaranteed.

'A only if B' means A implies B. 'Unless' means 'if not'. To show that 'if P then Q' is false, you need one case where P is true and Q is false.
cards.definition:
$$P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$$

Converse: Q ⇒ P (not equivalent). Inverse: ¬P ⇒ ¬Q (not equivalent, but equivalent to the converse).

Chain: if P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ R then P ⇒ R.

Negation: ¬(P ⇒ Q) is 'P and not Q'.

Symbols: ⇒ means 'implies', ¬ means 'not'. 'P only if Q' means P ⇒ Q.
cards.intuition_full: A promise 'if P then Q' is broken only when P happens and Q does not. So whenever Q fails, P cannot have happened, otherwise the promise would be broken. That is the contrapositive. The converse reads the promise backwards. A wet ground does not tell you what caused it, since the promise says rain forces wet but does not say only rain makes things wet. Chains work like dominoes: P knocks Q, Q knocks R, so P knocks R. And if R stays standing, then Q did not fall, and P did not either. To disprove a promise, find a single counterexample: P true and Q false. A penguin disproves 'if it is a bird, it can fly'.

example.setup: Rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. We learn that R is false. What follows about Q and P?
steps: Two rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. Each arrow is a one-way promise.
Suppose we learn that R is false.
Then Q must be false too. If Q were true, the arrow Q implies R would force R true.
Same step again: if P were true, Q would be true. So P is false. Not R leads to not P.
The contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P'. The converse, 'Q implies P', is a different claim and is not guaranteed.
example.answer: Q is false and P is false.

examples.setup: Rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. We learn that R is false. What follows about Q and P?
steps: Two rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. Each arrow is a one-way promise.
Suppose we learn that R is false.
Then Q must be false too. If Q were true, the arrow Q implies R would force R true.
Same step again: if P were true, Q would be true. So P is false. Not R leads to not P.
The contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P'. The converse, 'Q implies P', is a different claim and is not guaranteed.
examples.answer: Q is false and P is false.

examples.setup: 'A student can sit the exam only if attendance is at least 75%.' Ria sat the exam. Meena has 80% attendance. What can be concluded about each?
steps: Rewrite: sat the exam implies attendance at least 75%.
Ria sat the exam, so her attendance is at least 75%.
Meena has 80% attendance, which satisfies the condition, but the rule says only that attendance is necessary.
Nothing follows about whether Meena sat the exam. That would be the converse.
examples.answer: Ria's attendance is at least 75%. Nothing follows about Meena sitting the exam.

examples.setup: Which single example shows that 'if it is a bird, it can fly' is false? (a sparrow / a penguin / a bat / a stone)
steps: The statement is false only when P is true and Q is false: a bird that cannot fly.
A sparrow is a bird that flies, which fits the rule.
A bat flies but is not a bird, and a stone is not a bird. They are irrelevant, since P is false.
A penguin is a bird that cannot fly: P true, Q false.

cards.why: Conditionals are the formal core of logic and a recurring GATE pattern. The contrapositive is the only safe backward step. In GATE: given a rule, decide what must follow from a fact, or which statement is not necessarily true.
how: Write the rule as P implies Q, translating 'only if' and 'unless'.
Flip and negate to get the contrapositive.
Reject the converse and the inverse.
For chains, link the arrows. To disprove, find P true with Q false.
cards.mistake: Treating the converse as equivalent. 'If it rains the ground is wet' does not give 'if the ground is wet it rained'. Use the contrapositive instead: dry ground means no rain.
edge_cases: 'P only if Q' is P implies Q, not Q implies P.
'Unless Q, P' means 'if not Q then P'.
A false P makes 'P implies Q' true regardless of Q.
'If and only if' is true in both directions.
connections: Syllogisms (n2) are 'all' statements, which are conditionals.
Truth puzzles (n5) use the same case logic.
Discrete logic (dm.logic) gives the formal truth tables.

check.q: 'If it is a square, it has four sides.' A shape has three sides. What follows?
'If it is a square, it has four sides.' A shape has four sides. Must it be a square?
What is the contrapositive of 'if I study, I pass'?
check.a: If I do not pass, I did not study.

cards.what: Two rules: if P then Q, and if Q then R. Suppose we learn R is false. Then Q must be false, because Q true would force R true. And then P must be false for the same reason. The safe backward step is the **contrapositive**: not Q implies not P. The converse, Q implies P, is a different claim and is not guaranteed.
cards.what_full:
Two rules: if P then Q, and if Q then R. Suppose we learn R is false. Then Q must be false, because Q true would force R true. And then P must be false for the same reason. The safe backward step is the **contrapositive**: not Q implies not P. The converse, Q implies P, is a different claim and is not guaranteed.

'A only if B' means A implies B. 'Unless' means 'if not'. To show that 'if P then Q' is false, you need one case where P is true and Q is false.

$$P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$$

Converse: Q ⇒ P (not equivalent). Inverse: ¬P ⇒ ¬Q (not equivalent, but equivalent to the converse).

Chain: if P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ R then P ⇒ R.

Negation: ¬(P ⇒ Q) is 'P and not Q'.

Symbols: ⇒ means 'implies', ¬ means 'not'. 'P only if Q' means P ⇒ Q.

**Worked example.** Rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. We learn that R is false. What follows about Q and P?

1. Two rules: P implies Q, and Q implies R. Each arrow is a one-way promise.
2. Suppose we learn that R is false.
3. Then Q must be false too. If Q were true, the arrow Q implies R would force R true.
4. Same step again: if P were true, Q would be true. So P is false. Not R leads to not P.
5. The contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P'. The converse, 'Q implies P', is a different claim and is not guaranteed.

**Answer:** Q is false and P is false.

**Check yourself:** 'If it is a square, it has four sides.' A shape has three sides. What follows?

*Answer:* It is not a square.

What comes after 2, 5, 10, 17, 26? First try the gaps between neighbours.
Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. They are not constant, so it is not a plain add-the-same rule.
Differences of the differences: 2, 2, 2. A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern.
Extend from the bottom. The second difference stays 2.
So the next first difference is 9 + 2 = 11.
The next term is 26 + 11 = 37. These are n squared + 1: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37.

scenes.title: Name the link, then reuse it

objects.text:
Feather: wrong direction
Sky, Fly: only same topic

steps.caption: Name the link of the first pair: a tail is a part of a dog. Part to whole.
Apply to the second pair: a wing is a part of what whole?
Bird is the whole. Feather is a part of a wing, which is the wrong direction. Sky and fly are only related by topic.
Choose bird.  **Answer:** Bird.

scenes.title: All roses are flowers, all flowers are plants

objects.text:
I. roses are plants
true in every picture

II. plants are roses
false: grass is a plant

steps.caption: Draw the roses circle inside the flowers circle.
Draw the flowers circle inside the plants circle.
So roses lie inside plants: Conclusion I holds in every picture.
Plants can contain things that are not roses, such as grass. So II fails in a legitimate picture.  **Answer:** Only I follows.

scenes.title: Try each case; keep the one with no contradiction

steps.caption: Assume A is a knight. Then A's statement is true, so B is a knave.

set.text:
A knight: A's statement is true,
so B is a knave

steps.caption: B is a knave, so B's statement is false: it is not true that both are knights. This is consistent, since A is a knight and B is a knave.

set.text:
B knave: B's claim is false,
as a knave's claim should be

steps.caption: Try the other case: A is a knave. Then B is not a knave, so B is a knight, and B's statement says both are knights, but A is a knave. Contradiction.

set.text:
A knave: B is a knight, but B's
claim 'both knights' is false

steps.caption: Only the first assignment survives.  **Answer:** A is a knight and B is a knave.

set.text: A is a knight and B is a knave

List the routes from A to D: A-B-D, A-C-D, A-C-B-D.

scenes.title: Walk the family tree: up, then across

steps.caption: Draw B at the bottom.
Go up one step to B's mother.
Go sideways to her brother, who is A.
The path is up, across: A is B's maternal uncle.  **Answer:** Maternal uncle.
